title: The serpent (Genesis 3:1–7)
hook: did God really say, and the fruit that looked good

segments.voice: Yesterday, not good to be alone, ezer kenegdo: the first not good, and an equal who stands facing him. Who did you pull one step in? Today, the garden gets a visitor. Day three hundred thirty-eight.
screen: `BONE OF MY BONES, FLESH OF MY FLESH.`

segments.voice: Plenty of paintings of this scene share the same props: a tree, a woman reaching up, a shiny red apple, maybe a snake curled around a branch, with a face. Open Genesis and look for the apple. It isn't there. The text just says fruit. Some readers think the apple grew later, in art, perhaps helped along by a Latin pun: malum means evil, and malum also means apple. The real story is quieter and stranger than the paintings. It doesn't start with a bite. It starts with a question.
screen: `A TREE, A WOMAN, A RED APPLE.` → `THE TEXT SAYS ONLY FRUIT.` → `IT STARTS WITH A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The serpent, Genesis says, was more subtle than any of the beasts. And its first words are a question. In the Douay-Rheims: "Why hath God commanded you, that you should not eat of every tree of paradise?" Other translations put it more sharply: did God really say? Notice the trick. God had said they could eat of every tree but one. The serpent turns the one limit into the whole story. The woman corrects it, but now the doubt is in the air. Then the serpent goes further: you won't die; God knows that you'll be like gods. That's the shape of temptation the Church sees here. First, the question that shrinks the gift and enlarges the rule. Second, the suspicion: maybe God is holding out on you. Third, the look. The woman sees that the tree is good to eat, fair to the eyes, and desirable for wisdom. Everything about it looks good. In the story, the wrong choice shows up looking good. Fourth, the result. She eats, gives some to her husband, who is with her, and he eats. Their eyes are opened, but what they see is only that they're naked. They sew fig leaves. The Catechism reads this as the first sin: letting trust in God die in the heart, and wanting to be like God without God. It uses figurative language, the Catechism says, but it tells of a real event at the start of human history. And Genesis never names the serpent. Later scripture fills that in: the Book of Wisdom says death came into the world by the envy of the devil, and Revelation calls the devil that old serpent.
screen: `A QUESTION THAT SHRINKS THE GIFT.` · `MAYBE GOD IS HOLDING OUT.` · `IT LOOKS GOOD TO THE EYES.` · `TRUST DIES BEFORE THE BITE.` · then, large: `DID GOD REALLY SAY?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one small temptation's voice. Settle, and breathe. Think of something small you keep doing that you'd rather not: the third episode, the snapped reply, the extra purchase, the scroll at midnight. Now listen for the sentence that comes right before it. It's usually reasonable. You deserve this. It doesn't really matter. Nobody will know. Just hear it, without arguing back. Notice how gentle it sounds. If you pray, you can ask for help to recognize it next time. The bell holds the time.
Temptation. Being drawn toward a wrong that looks good. In the garden it starts with a question that makes the gift look small and the limit look huge.
Your line: did god really say. Today, when a little voice says the rule doesn't count this time, name the trick to yourself, and pause for three breaths. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics pray "lead us not into temptation" in every Our Father, and the Church reads Genesis 3 on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, as Lent begins.

fork.setup: you're in the garden. a voice asks why God won't let you eat of every tree. you know you can eat of all but one. what happens in the story?
options: the woman ignores the question and walks away.
the woman corrects it, but the doubt stays, and she looks again at the tree.
fork.reveal: she corrects the serpent, but the question has done its work. she sees the fruit is good to eat and fair to the eyes, and eats, and gives to her husband.

original.note: Hebrew: serpent, snake. Genesis gives it no other name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about an apple and a snake.
what it means: temptation starts with a question that makes God's gift look small, and trust dies before the bite.
what a scholar hears: the apple may have grown from art and a Latin pun, malum, evil and apple; the Catechism reads the scene as figurative language for a real first sin.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 3:1 quoted from memory; confirm wording and punctuation.

'Did God really say?': the carry follows the index; it's the sense of the Hebrew and the wording of several modern translations, not the Douay-Rheims. The script says 'other translations put it more sharply' without naming any. Confirm.
Apple and the malum pun: a common explanation, softened to 'perhaps helped along by'. Confirm.
CCC 390 (figurative language, primeval event), CCC 397 (letting trust die), CCC 398 (wanting to be like God without God). Paraphrased; confirm.
